---
title: "Label retrieval"
description: "Choose ROC or precision-recall AUC and inspect overall, per-label, and per-query retrieval scores."
---

Use this guide when known labels define what should be retrieved near each
observation. Choose ROC AUC for rank discrimination across relevant and
irrelevant candidates. Prefer PR AUC when relevant observations are rare and
precision among retrieved observations matters.

`roc_auc()` and `pr_auc()` treat each observation as a query, rank the remaining
observations by distance, and regard matching labels as relevant. These are
supervised retrieval summaries. Both functions require the
[PRROC package](https://cran.r-project.org/package=PRROC).
[Venna and colleagues](https://jmlr.org/papers/v11/venna10a.html) develop the retrieval view of
dimensionality-reduction evaluation. [Bamber](https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-2496(75)90001-2)
relates ROC area to ranking probability. For each query, Quadra uses PRROC's
[Davis–Goadrich PR area](https://doi.org/10.1145/1143844.1143874).

Perfect retrieval has AUC 1 for both measures. Random ROC AUC is 0.5. The random
PR AUC baseline is the prevalence of relevant observations among the remaining
candidates, so it changes with label imbalance.

```{r label-retrieval-setup}
library(quadra)

iris_x <- as.matrix(iris[, -5])
pca_iris <- stats::prcomp(iris_x, retx = TRUE, rank. = 2)$x
dout <- as.matrix(stats::dist(pca_iris))
```

```{r overall-and-label-auc}
roc <- roc_auc(dout, iris$Species)
pr <- pr_auc(dout, iris$Species)

auc_summary <- rbind(
  ROC = c(overall = roc$av_auc, unlist(roc$label_av)),
  PR = c(overall = pr$av_auc, unlist(pr$label_av))
)
signif(auc_summary, 5)
```

```{r overall-and-label-auc-check, include=FALSE}
iris_pr_baseline <- (table(iris$Species) - 1) / (nrow(iris) - 1)
stopifnot(
  identical(colnames(auc_summary), c("overall", levels(iris$Species))),
  all(is.finite(auc_summary)),
  all(auc_summary >= 0 & auc_summary <= 1),
  roc$av_auc > 0.5,
  all(unlist(pr$label_av) > iris_pr_baseline),
  all(auc_summary[, "setosa"] > 0.999),
  all(auc_summary[, "setosa"] < 1),
  all(
    sweep(
      auc_summary[, c("versicolor", "virginica"), drop = FALSE],
      1,
      auc_summary[, "setosa"],
      FUN = "<"
    )
  )
)
```

Every Iris class has 50 observations, so each query has 49 relevant candidates
among the other 149 and a random PR baseline of about 0.329. The overall Iris
scores are above their random baselines. Setosa is retrieved almost perfectly
in this PCA embedding; for versicolor and virginica, same-label observations
are less consistently ranked ahead of the other classes. The difference
between ROC and PR values is not itself a winner-takes-all comparison: the
measures use different baselines and emphasize different retrieval behavior.

## Inspecting Query-Level Results

By default, each function returns `list(av_auc, label_av)`. `av_auc` weights
each defined query equally; `label_av` contains per-label means in
first-appearance order. Set `ret_extra = TRUE` to append the row-aligned
`query_auc` vector and its defined-query count.

```{r query-level-auc}
roc_detail <- roc_auc(dout, iris$Species, ret_extra = TRUE)
head(round(roc_detail$query_auc, 3))
roc_detail$n_defined
```

```{r query-level-auc-check, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(
  length(roc_detail$query_auc) == nrow(iris),
  roc_detail$n_defined == nrow(iris),
  all(is.finite(roc_detail$query_auc)),
  all(roc_detail$query_auc >= 0 & roc_detail$query_auc <= 1)
)
```

All 150 Iris queries are defined. In other data, queries without both relevant
and irrelevant candidates are `NA_real_` and excluded from the overall and
per-label means. If no query is defined, the overall average is `NA_real_`.

Both functions require a finite square distance matrix and one nonmissing label
per observation. The query itself is excluded from its ranking. Labels without
a defined query remain `NA_real_` in `label_av`.

## Find which class pairs changed

Per-label AUC can tell you that retrieval got worse. Restrict the candidates to two classes to
see which labels became harder to tell apart.

Start with four separated copies of a small grid. In one output, move the grids in each column
onto one another. In the other, do the same within each row.

```{r label-pair-example}
tile <- as.matrix(expand.grid(x = c(-0.125, 0, 0.125), y = c(-0.125, 0, 0.125)))
label <- rep(LETTERS[1:4], each = nrow(tile))
make_distances <- function(cx, cy) {
  xy <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(cx), function(i) {
    sweep(tile, 2, c(cx[i], cy[i]), "+")
  }))
  as.matrix(dist(xy))
}
din <- make_distances(c(0, 0, 4, 4), c(0, 4, 0, 4))
merge_columns <- make_distances(c(0, 0, 4, 4), c(0, 0, 0, 0))
merge_rows <- make_distances(c(0, 0, 0, 0), c(0, 4, 0, 4))

pr_by_label <- function(d) unlist(pr_auc(d, label)$label_av)
round(rbind(columns = pr_by_label(merge_columns), rows = pr_by_label(merge_rows)), 3)
```

Both outputs give the same PR AUC for each label. Now compare two-class ROC AUC in the input and
in each output, using the same query and candidate IDs for each pair.

```{r label-pair-roc}
reference <- class_pair_auc(din, label, metrics = "roc")
data.frame(
  reference,
  column_merge_change = round(class_pair_auc(merge_columns, label, "roc")$roc - reference$roc, 3),
  row_merge_change = round(class_pair_auc(merge_rows, label, "roc")$roc - reference$roc, 3)
)
```

The negative rows identify the pairs that were merged. Positive changes in other comparisons
mean retrieval became easier between those labels. That can help flag separation exaggerated
by an embedding. [Jeon et al. on class-pair distortion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.00278)

## Which centroid is closer? {#compare-centroid-separation}

Take just the 5s and 9s. What fraction of these images are closer to their own digit's centroid
than to the other one? A tie counts as half. `label_trustworthiness_continuity()` compares that
fraction in the input and the embedding for each pair of labels. Trustworthiness penalizes a drop.
Continuity penalizes a rise, since the map can also make the classes look *more* distinct than
they were. In PCA the 5s and 9s get easier to retrieve even as fewer images lie closer to their own
centroid. [Jeon and colleagues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.00278) compare class-pair changes using
distance consistency, introduced by
[Sips and colleagues](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8659.2009.01467.x).
Quadra uses the unrescaled fraction. Jeon and colleagues provide their
[implementation](https://github.com/hj-n/ltnc).
[MNIST example](mnist-pca-umap.html#compare-pairs-of-digits)

## Compare class angular spread

`class_angular_distortion_index()` compares the angles between pairs of points from one class as
seen from points in another class. Its detailed results report each direction separately, so
you can see whether one class's apparent spread changes more than the other's. Use the sampled
triplet counts to check how much evidence each direction has.
[Gunaratne, Kobourov and Miller introduce CADI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.00637). Quadra follows
the normalization in their [code](https://github.com/KaviruGunaratne/cadi). Their sampler picks
classes first. Quadra samples eligible triplets uniformly, so class sizes affect the overall score.
[MNIST example](mnist-pca-umap.html#compare-angular-spread-from-each-digit)
